article.title: What Does a Reinsurance Broker Do? Interview w/ Howden Re Managing Director of Broking Josephine Li
article.preview: Insurance is a critical component of life in today's world. You buy insurance to protect yourself and your assets, be that health, your car, your home, your possessions, and more. Businesses and even
article.text:
Insurance is a critical component of life in today's world. You buy insurance to protect yourself and your assets, be that health, your car, your home, your possessions, and more. Businesses and even governments do the same.
But insurers need insurance too. That’s why they seek out reinsurance: insurance for insurers. Hardly anyone outside of the insurance world will ever see it, but it’s critical to the industry at large.
When insurers seek reinsurance, it’s the reinsurance brokers who do the legwork. They’re involved from start to finish in arranging the deals, and their work continues well after the contract is signed.
Josephine Li, ACAS, is managing director of broking at Howden Re, one of the world’s leading reinsurance brokerages. In this interview, she discusses the role of a broker, what a deal involves, and her experience working with Cover Re.
The work and the person behind it
The role of a reinsurance broker draws on expertise in risk, negotiation, analysis, and industry knowledge. Brokers act as the primary channel through which insurers seek out reinsurance, helping them determine suitable reinsurers, negotiate the terms, and then manage the ongoing work after a contract is signed. Josephine’s experience offers a view into the profession, including her path into broking, what the work involves, and the lessons she’s learned about building relationships and a career in reinsurance.
For readers who’ve never met a reinsurance broker, how do you describe your job at a dinner party?
We help insurance companies insure themselves. A reinsurance broker is part strategist, part translator and part negotiator. We help clients understand the risks they’re taking, decide how much of that risk they want to keep, and find capital to take the rest.
What does a typical day actually look like for you right now?
There really isn’t one. I can go from talking with a client about growth or capital strategy, to working through analytics and treaty structure, to negotiating with reinsurers, to getting different internal teams aligned around a placement. A lot of the job is connecting the technical, commercial and relationship pieces.
You have an actuarial background. How does someone go from the actuarial track to broking, and what made you make that jump?
The actuarial background gave me a very strong foundation for deconstructing risk and testing whether the economics make sense. What attracted me to broking was being able to take that analytical foundation and add strategy, negotiation, clients and the market. I liked being closer to the decisions rather than only analyzing them after the fact.
What’s the moment you knew reinsurance was going to be your career? Was there a deal, a mentor, a market event?
It wasn’t one dramatic moment. I stumbled into reinsurance after college, but I stayed because the problems kept being interesting and no two deals were ever exactly the same.
What’s the hardest lesson the market has taught you? A deal that went sideways, a renewal you lost, a call you got wrong?
Being technically right isn’t enough. You have to understand what motivates everyone involved, communicate clearly, get the timing right and know when to push versus when to listen. And when you do get something wrong, owning it quickly matters a lot more than trying to defend it.
Reinsurance is a relationship business. How did you build your book of relationships when you were starting out, before you had a track record?
By being useful. When you’re early in your career, you may not have decades of relationships or a big book, but you can be prepared, responsive, curious and dependable. If people learn that when they call you they’ll get a thoughtful answer and you’ll do what you said you were going to do, the relationships build from there.
What’s a misconception about brokers (even inside the industry) that you’d like to correct?
That the job is primarily matchmaking, take a risk from a client and find someone willing to write it. The best broking is much more consultative than that. A good broker should be helping shape the risk, challenge assumptions, improve the structure, create competition and ultimately help both sides make a better decision.
What advice would you give someone considering a move into broking today?
Learn the fundamentals first. Understand analytics, contracts, how your client makes money and how the reinsurer makes money. Then learn how to explain complicated things simply. The people who can combine technical credibility with judgment, communication and relationships become very valuable very quickly.
How a reinsurance deal comes together
A reinsurance deal begins with establishing the insurer’s specific goals. The broker then works through the insurer’s data, develops potential contract structures, and approaches potential reinsurers to seek feedback and negotiate. After the agreement is signed, the broker continues working with both sides on contract issues, amendments, and premium and claims activity throughout the life of the treaty.
Josephine describes how that process unfolds in practice: the preparation behind a deal, and the factors she considers when selecting a reinsurer.
Walk me through a deal from the very first conversation to binding. Where does a treaty actually begin (a phone call, a renewal date, a lunch)?
The treaty usually starts with a business problem, not a treaty structure. You first understand what the client is trying to accomplish, growth, capital relief, earnings protection, something else. Then you work through the data and modeling, develop structures, build the underwriting story, approach the right markets, take feedback, negotiate terms and capacity, allocate the line and ultimately bind it. The structure is really the output of understanding the underlying problem.
 
Matchmaking is the visible part of broking. What’s the invisible part, like the work clients and reinsurers never see?
A huge amount of preparation. It’s understanding the portfolio, pressure-testing the analytics, anticipating reinsurer questions, figuring out which markets are genuinely relevant, managing competing interests and sometimes solving problems before the client ever knows they existed. The meeting or negotiation is the visible 10%; most of the work happened before anyone got into the room.
When you’re deciding which reinsurer to bring a client’s risk to, what are you actually weighing? What separates a market you trust from one you don’t?
Price and capacity obviously matter, but they’re only part of it. I’m looking at underwriting appetite, financial strength, expertise, responsiveness, consistency and whether I believe they’ll still behave like a partner when something goes wrong. A market earns trust through what it does after the easy part of the transaction is over.
Once a treaty is bound, you service it for its whole life. What does that actually involve month to month, and why does it matter so much?
Binding isn’t the end of the relationship. There are contract issues, data, premium and loss activity, claims, amendments, changing exposures and ongoing conversations with both sides throughout the year. Good servicing also makes the next renewal better because nobody wants to rediscover the relationship once a year.
Working with Cover Re
Howden Re is Cover Re’s largest broker relationship. Josephine shares her first impressions of Cover Re, her experience working with its technical team, and what Cover Re has done to secure repeat business with Howden.
Do you remember the first Cover Re deal you worked on? What was your honest first impression of them as a market?
What stood out was that you were innovative without treating innovation as a substitute for underwriting. There are plenty of new ideas around capital and technology, but ultimately this business still comes down to understanding risk, pricing it appropriately and honoring your commitments.
Is there a moment in the relationship that stands out?
The team’s technical capability stands out, especially in structured markets. Jon [Lim, chief underwriting officer) and Blanca [Qin, head of underwriting] are very strong technicians in their respective areas, which makes conversations about structure mechanics much smoother. It feels more like a thoughtful debate with knowledgeable peers than having to explain how each part of the deal mechanics works.
Howden is now Cover Re’s largest broker relationship. From your side of the table, what has Cover Re done to earn repeat business? What does “reliable execution” actually look like in practice?
Engage early, give useful feedback, give a clear yes or no, make decisions when you say you will and don’t change the rules late in the process. If a reinsurer consistently does those things, brokers remember it.
How the market is changing
The reinsurance industry is drawing upon an increasingly varied mix of capital: not just traditional reinsurers and private capital, but also newer technology-enabled approaches such as Re. Josephine discusses where those changes could lead, the potential role of crypto-native capital, and what participants on both sides need to understand about each other.
You sit at a vantage point where you see the whole market. What’s changing in reinsurance right now that you find most interesting, or most worrying?
I think the variety of capital entering the market is fascinating. You have traditional balance-sheet reinsurers, ILS capital, private capital and increasingly technology-enabled approaches all looking at similar risks in different ways. That creates more options for clients, but it also means brokers have to understand the differences between sources of capital rather than treating capacity as interchangeable.
New sources of capital keep entering the market. Where do you think that goes in the next 5-10 years? Is crypto-native capital a novelty or the beginning of something structural?
I think it’s part of a broader structural trend toward new forms of capital entering insurance and reinsurance. The technology itself is interesting, but what ultimately determines whether any new source of capital lasts is much more traditional: permanence, control, liquidity, how it performs through losses, and whether policyholders and cedants have appropriate protections. If it can pass those tests, then it becomes less about “crypto” and more about another credible source of risk capital.
What would you say to a traditional insurance person who’s skeptical of protocols like Re? And conversely, what should crypto people understand about how this market really works?
To the traditional insurance side, I’d say don’t dismiss a new mechanism simply because the technology is unfamiliar. But the reverse is equally important: technology doesn’t eliminate underwriting cycles, claims development or the importance of trust. Insurance has accumulated a lot of institutional knowledge for good reasons.
Finish this sentence: “The best brokers are the ones who ______.”
…create outcomes where both sides win.
Many thanks to Josephine for taking the time to share her experience and perspective! Learn more about Josephine on LinkedIn.

article.title: Claims, Costs, and Premiums: Understanding Reinsurance Treaty Performance

article.text:
Reinsurance, like any other area of finance, is a for-profit business. Reinsurers carefully select, price, and negotiate treaties with an eye toward one primary goal: fulfilling their obligations to the insurer while maximizing margins. For the average reinsurer, that means greater value for shareholders. For Re, underwriting profits support yield for holders of reUSD and reUSDe.
But what goes into determining the profit equation? What costs and revenues go into it? And how is the result measured? Let’s explore.
The Treaty
Before any money changes hands, the terms of the deal have to be set. That's the role of the reinsurance treaty: the contract between insurer and reinsurer. It determines what business is covered, how much risk the reinsurer takes on, how the reinsurer will be compensated for taking that risk, and under what circumstances it will be responsible for losses.
Some treaties may include caps on what the reinsurer is expected to pay, while others will not. Some require reinsurers to pay out a portion of covered losses from the start, whereas others may require insured losses to reach a certain level first. The exact details can vary widely, but the basic purpose is the same.
The Considerations
When deciding upon a treaty, the reinsurer must answer two questions: is this risk worth taking? And if so, what premium should we charge for it?
A lot goes into this decision. For example:
Historical loss data: how often has this type of claim occurred, and what did it cost when it did?
Risk models: statistical tools that estimate the probability and severity of future losses.
Exposure data: the specific characteristics of the risk being covered (such as vehicle types, geographic area, industry classification, or workforce size).
Market benchmarks: what are other reinsurers charging for similar risks, and why?
Let’s look at commercial auto, Re’s second largest category of business (as of October 2026). Before backing commercial auto business, reinsurance underwriters will analyze the likes of fleet size, vehicle types, and their primary use; operating locations (urban routes generally see more accidents than rural ones); the insurer’s claims history over the long term; and the financial health of the insurer itself.
The goal is to build an accurate picture of how likely claims are to occur, how expensive they will be, and, above all, whether the premium justifies the risk. The premium must be high enough to cover expected claims and operating costs yet still generate a good return for the reinsurers.
In the end, the performance of a treaty comes down to a simple comparison: how much money the reinsurer earned in premiums versus the amount it had to pay out in costs.
The Costs
Claims
When one thinks about insurance (and thus, by relation, about reinsurance), the primary cost one probably considers is claims. Policyholders file claims when covered events occur, and the insurer pays out based on the terms of the policy. It’s much the same for reinsurers; when events covered by a reinsurance treaty transpire, the reinsurer pays the insurer based on the letter of the contract between them.
But the claims category doesn't just include the cost of paying out those claims. It also includes the costs associated with those claims. For example, processing claims could require paying for defense lawyers, expert witnesses, fraud investigators, forensic accountants, court costs, and so on. There’s also the overhead of having a claims department at all: staff salaries, general infrastructure, even the office they work in.
Other Expenses
In addition to claims, there are the more ordinary expenses. Running an enterprise costs money, from the investment involved in finding business to the more mundane costs of operation. These are what you’d expect: they range from the likes of rent, utilities, and building maintenance, to furniture, equipment, computers and software, to cloud hosting, tax preparation, outside legal counsel, and staff salaries. They may also extend to reinsurance broker fees, costs associated with treaty negotiation, financial audits, and so on.
The Revenue
Revenue from reinsurance contracts comes from insurer premiums. Just as insurers receive premiums from policyholders for providing coverage, so do reinsurers from insurers. How much the reinsurer is paid depends on the terms of the treaty and can vary widely.
Premiums represent the revenue side of the underwriting performance equation. When determining underwriting performance, all costs are measured against them.
The Results
This brings us to the most important metric in reinsurance economics: the combined ratio. It’s the chief indicator of underwriting profitability (or lack thereof).
Combined ratio is a simple equation: add together claims and other expenses, then divide that sum by premiums taken in, and convert the result into a percentage.
Let’s say that for a given treaty, claims equaled $5 million, other expenses added another $4 million, and premiums were $10 million. That would yield a combined ratio of 90%, indicating that an underwriting profit was made. In simple terms, the reinsurer earned a dollar of premium for every 90 cents it spent on the treaty.
 
It’s rare for a reinsurer to carry just a single treaty. Reinsurers vary widely in size; most may carry dozens, hundreds, or even (in the case of the real titans) thousands of treaties at any given time. For any reinsurer, the most important manifestation of combined ratio isn’t the performance of any given treaty but rather that of their portfolio as a whole. That bundles together the performance of all treaties in the reinsurer’s book. 100% means that the reinsurer broke even. Over 100% equals a loss. Less than 100% means an underwriting profit.
 
Re’s Performance
To date, Re’s portfolio has been profitable (that is, a combined ratio of below 100%) in each individual year since inception. Since inception, it has recorded an overall combined ratio of 92%¹.
92%¹ Overall combined ratio since inception
Several factors help to explain that performance. First, a skilled and diligent underwriting team. Second, favoring meaningfully high loss thresholds (where applicable) before Re begins paying for losses. And finally, a highly diversified portfolio with only modest exposure to catastrophe.
¹ Past performance is not a reliable indicator of future results.
 
Read the Data
Traditional reinsurance is opaque. Treaty details rarely travel much beyond the insurer and reinsurer. They almost invariably aren’t available to the public.
Re takes a different approach. Those who provide capital to the portfolio have a detailed view into how that capital is being utilized, from overall strategy to details and performance data on each individual treaty, including premium, posted collateral, projected losses, and combined ratio.
For that information and more, check out the Re App.

article.text:
September brought two more major milestones for Re: total deposits across reUSD and reUSDe passed $300 million, and cumulative yield generated for holders exceeded $10 million.
The month also brought continued expansion on both sides of the business. Re added three new lines of business to its reinsurance portfolio, while reUSD added new markets across Exponent and Fluid.
$712.25M - Total Value Locked
+9.8% - TVL Growth
$318.4M - Total Deposits
$10M+ - Cumulative Yield Generated
Capital Position & Liquidity
All figures reflect the September 30, 2026, reporting snapshot unless otherwise noted. Past performance is not a reliable indicator of future results.
Re’s TVL stood at $712.25 million on September 30, an increase of 9.8% over August.
As of the reporting period, TVL was composed as follows:
$210.14M (29.5% of total assets) is held onchain to support Re-backed underwriting structures.
$183.18M (25.7% of total) is maintained offchain as reserves within regulated insurance entities.
$318.93M (44.8% of total) is composed of contracted written premium receivable. (Reflects contracted premium receivable on policies bound as of the reporting date. Actual receipts may vary based on policy performance, cessions, and other factors.)
As in August, capital growth was driven primarily by large-scale gains in reUSD deposits.
Deposits Passed $300 Million
August was marked by strong growth in total deposits. September saw that trend continue. Total deposits across reUSD and reUSDe increased from $256.4 million at the end of August to $318.4 million at the end of September, a gain of $62.0 million (24.2%).
Total Deposits: $256.4M → $318.4M
reUSD: $236.4M → $297.8M
reUSDe: $20.0M → $20.6M
The increase was driven in its vast majority by deposits in reUSD, which grew from $236.4 million to $297.8 million. reUSDe deposits increased from $20.0 million to $20.6 million.
Total deposits measure the combined value of all reUSD and reUSDe in circulation. Unlike TVL, the figure excludes premium receivable and capital held outside the circulating token supply.
Total Yield Generated Exceeded $10 Million
September included another milestone: cumulative yield generated for reUSD and reUSDe holders passed the $10 million mark.
Both tokens accrue yield through increases in NAV. Yield is primarily driven by licensed reinsurance activity.
Deposits measure the capital users have brought into the protocol; cumulative yield provides a separate measure of what that capital has generated for holders over time.
Portfolio Composition
Re added three new treaties during September, expanding Re’s underwriting portfolio into three additional areas of business:
Specialty auto - insurance for business vehicles and fleets with specialized risks that may not fit standard commercial auto coverage
Professional lines for startups - insurance covering business risks such as professional mistakes, management decisions, and other liabilities faced by startups
Large excess casualty - insurance for very large liability claims against businesses, including major accidents, injuries, and lawsuits
The new treaties brought inception-to-date bound premium to $510.6 million.
The addition of new categories further diversifies Re’s portfolio. Greater diversification reduces the chances that losses in any one area will coincide with losses elsewhere, limiting the impact that poor performance in any single category of business can have on the portfolio as a whole.
Though these new lines involve longer-duration risks, they make up only a small share of Re’s portfolio. Underwriting strategy continues to favor two primary characteristics: shorter-duration risks, and contracts that only begin paying after losses cross a meaningful threshold. This strategy is intended to help guard against losses and emphasize consistency in underwriting performance.
Ecosystem Expansion
September also brought additions to reUSD markets.
@ExponentFinance: A December 2026 reUSD market went live on Exponent, including PT-reUSD for fixed-rate exposure through maturity, plus YT-reUSD and a reUSD liquidity pool.
@0xFluid: Re expanded its reUSD integration with Fluid on Arbitrum. New vaults went live for reUSD/USDC, reUSD/USDT, and reUSD-USDC LP/USDC.
$RE Token Activity
Per the standard ecosystem release schedule, 7.09 million $RE unlocked from the ecosystem allocation on September 18.
$RE has a fixed maximum supply of one billion tokens, with no ongoing inflation or perpetual emissions.

1B - Fixed maximum supply, no ongoing inflation
What’s Next
October 1 saw the opening of the second reUSDe redemption window. Redemption requests will be accepted through October 14, with redemptions claimable from October 15 through November 14.
We look forward to delivering our next update in November.
- Re Management Team

article.title: Connecting Morpho Vaults to Morpho Midnight
article.preview:
Morpho Vaults V2 (“Morpho Vaults”) are expanding the types of credit they can allocate to.
Today, Morpho Vaults allocate to variable-rate Morpho Blue markets. The Midnight Adapter will go live in Q4
article.text:
Morpho Vaults V2 (“Morpho Vaults”) are expanding the types of credit they can allocate to.
Today, Morpho Vaults allocate to variable-rate Morpho Blue markets. The Midnight Adapter will go live in Q4 2026, enabling all new and existing Morpho Vaults to allocate deposits into fixed rate Morpho Midnight (“Midnight”) Markets.
This opens Midnight to the $5B+ already held in Morpho Vaults. For lenders, it means that vaults can offer more predictable, fixed-rate yield for a set term, without having to manage positions themselves. For vaults, it opens up a new design space and greater differentiation.
New Design Space & Differentiation for Vaults
On Blue, vaults stand out through the markets they choose and the risk settings they use. Curators are largely choosing between the same underlying market structure and differentiating through market selection, allocation weight, and rebalancing.
The Midnight adapter changes that materially, opening up a new design space for Morpho Vaults:
Two market structures instead of one: By opening access to Midnight, vaults can be configured to allocate across both market structures (Blue & Midnight). This gives curators more ways to show the value of their vault setup.
Utilization and Liquidity Profile: Curators can allocate across Blue, Midnight and idle markets to shape a vault's utilization and liquidity profile. Midnight's fixed-term positions can enable a higher utilization and potentially high returns, but high utilization does not necessarily mean less is withdrawable. Blue allocations can benefit from shared market liquidity and keep a vault highly withdrawable, while Midnight allocations are shaped by their terms and maturities. Curators can use these different liquidity profiles to differentiate their vaults.
Vaults can set their own terms: On Morpho Blue, vaults receive the rate set by the market’s interest rate model. With Morpho Midnight, there is no formula. The curator configures the risk parameters and the given rate at which the vault is willing to accept.
The result is vault infrastructure that enables a high level of differentiation, not just from the type of collateral assets, but in pricing, term, and liquidity.
 
How Morpho Vaults handle Midnight positions
Midnight fixed-rate positions behave differently from variable-rate Blue positions. The design challenge was to enable the allocation from Morpho Vaults to Midnight while preserving the vaults’ noncustodial properties and user protections. As a result, the Midnight Adapter enforces the following:
Buying protections: A vault’s Midnight positions must stay within its exposure and maturity limits.
Selling protections: By default, a vault cannot sell a whole position for less than the amortized value. An exception to this would be subject to a timelock.
Caps: Every Midnight position counts against the vault’s caps on the things that define its risk, such as the collateral asset and its parameters. Curators can also cap how much of the vault is lent for longer periods, for example beyond 90 days. Caps can be lowered immediately, but increasing them is timelocked, so depositors can exit before any increase in risk applies.
In-kind redemptions: Users can exit a vault position into the underlying Midnight position, even when the vault has no idle liquidity, through in-kind redemptions.
Amortized valuation: Each position is valued at the amount due at maturity, discounted at its entry rate. Its value accrues steadily as maturity approaches.
Together, these design choices keep Morpho Vaults noncustodial and put predefined limits on the risks a vault can take with Midnight positions.
A defining change for Morpho Vaults & Midnight
The Midnight adapter is an important step in expanding Morpho Vaults beyond a single market structure, and opening $5B in liquidity to Midnight Markets.
Morpho Vaults will soon be able to allocate liquidity across both Morpho Blue’s open-ended, variable-rate markets and Midnight’s fixed-rate, fixed-term markets, giving users a choice of vaults with different liquidity and variable yield profiles.

article.text:
Curation is a high growth early-stage industry.
Two and a half years ago it barely existed as a business. Today roughly $10B sits in curated vaults.
Coinbase and Robinhood now run their earn products on them, and each passed $500M in deposits in September.
More than 30 curators are now active, including established names like Steakhouse Financial, Sentora, Gauntlet, and recent entrants like Galaxy Digital, Bitwise Asset Management and Armitage by Wintermute.
Underneath sit the vaults: the onchain infrastructure curators use to set risk parameters and allocation rules. A year ago we argued that vaults would become the default way to allocate liquidity onchain. That has become the consensus, and institutions are moving into the space.
But a vault has come to mean very different things, depending on the power of its curator. We think of it as a spectrum. On one end are noncustodial vaults, where the curator sets the rules but cannot change allocation without users consent or take control of user assets. On the other end are discretionary vaults, where the operator custody customer assets, and can move assets as they see fit to run more complex strategies.
Despite Morpho Vaults being designed as noncustodial, with the combination of in-kind redemptions, timelocks, role-based access controls and immutable contracts, the same open-source infrastructure could also be forked and configured to create something that looks more like a discretionary vault.
At the end of the day, there is no one size fits all. Different needs will require different vault infrastructure. The more diversity we have at the vault infrastructure layer, the more tools we have to bring all types of credit onchain. We believe the more diverse the vault ecosystem is, the more tools we have to bring all types of credit onchain.

@Ethereum is most neutral network with one of the deepest liquidity onchain. It brings more Midnight's fixed rate markets to users who have a mandate to allocate on Ethereum only. Midnight's crosschain expansion has just begun.
 
Direct Lend into Morpho Blue
Lending directly into Morpho Blue markets has always been possible by interacting with the smart contracts or through third-party apps such as Monarch Lend.
It is now available in the Morpho App, for users who are comfortable applying their own risk expertise.
 
Morpho is the credit infrastructure on Arc

Your stablecoins have more potential than waiting around for your next trade.

That's why Jupiter gives you over 7 different ways to earn on them:

1. Jupiter Lend Earn Vaults
Jupiter Lend lets you deposit USDC, JupUSD, and more into lending pools to earn interest from borrowers.

In return, you receive a receipt token that is indicated by a jl-prefix. In the case of USDC, you'd get jlUSDC.

As you earn interest, the value of the jl-Token grows without needing to manually claim your earnings.

You can also access Lend through Jupiter Mobile, or just swap in and out of jlTokens directly. 
 

2. Auto-Earn in Jupiter Wallet
An integration that deserves its own mention is the Auto-Earn feature on Jupiter Wallet. 

Toggle it on for specific stables, and your extension Wallet will automatically deposit your balance into Lend to start earning for you.
 

3. DCA Earn
If you're spreading your purchases out over time through Dollar Cost Averaging, your funds can earn while they wait.

When you use Jupiter DCA with USDC, USDT, or JupUSD you can toggle on a feature to earn yield via Jupiter Lend in between your buys.
 

4. Jupiter Lend Smart Vaults
Smart Vaults let paired assets serve as liquidity for Jupiter Lend AMM, earning fees from swaps.

In the case of Smart collateral, you supply a pair such as syrupUSDC-USDC and earn from a combination of lending interest, native token yield, and trading fees. 

You can deposit either token, and Jupiter automatically composes the pair for you at the pool's current ratio.
 

5. Lending or Longing through Jupiter Offerbook
Jupiter Offerbook gives you a couple different  options for your USDC, specifically.

Lend at a fixed rate: Fund an existing borrowing offer in USDC. If the borrower repays, you receive your funds back, plus interest. However, if they don’t repay after maturity, you can take their collateral.
Open a leveraged long: Deposit USDC to gain more exposure to a token's price action. To read more about leveraged longing with Offerbook, you can check out the docs.
 

6. Swapping into yield-bearing stables.
When you click the 'yield' category on Jupiter’s stablecoin screener page, you can find a large list of yield-bearing stables and dollar-denominated tokens.
 

7. Other ways to earn
For completeness, there are two additional options worth mentioning:
JLP: You can swap your stables into JLP, or mint it using supported assets such as USDC and JupUSD (when capacity allows).

JLP serves as the liquidity pool for Jupiter's JLP-based perps markets, and receives 75% of the fees generated. However, it also exposes you to a basket of assets including SOL, ETH, and BTC.
Perps Trading: Jupiter Perps Beta markets use USDC as the collateral asset, allowing you to long or short ZEC, Hype, JUP, SNDK, SPCX, or SKHYNIX.
But do note: The risk profile for perps is different compared to something like lending mentioned above. Market moves against your position can potentially cause a liquidation.
 

Activate your Stables
Whether you want hands-off background yield with Auto-Earn, fixed rates on Offerbook, or more active strategies via Perps, Jupiter has an outlet for your specific risk tolerance.
But regardless of what you choose, stop letting your stables sit on the sidelines.

You can Stake your JUP to earn Active Staking Rewards (ASR) while gaining voting power in the DAO.

Over 1.12 Billion JUP is currently staked, earning an estimated APY of 17.8%.

Your share of JUP rewards is time-weighted, meaning it depends how much you've staked and for how long.

Voting isn't required, but your stake also gives you a say whenever proposals come up.
 

2. Borrowing Stables 
Want access to liquidity while maintaining your JUP exposure?

Jupiter Lend lets you supply JUP as collateral and borrow USDC or USDT against it. 

You can then use those funds elsewhere in DeFi, whether you're pursuing yield or preparing for your next trade.

You have to pay interest on what you borrow, and your position can experience a liquidation if your collateral value drops too far.

Just make sure to keep an eye on your position health.
 

3. Borrow, Lend, or go Long via Offerbook.
Jupiter Offerbook gives you 3 different ways to participate in the JUP market.

Borrow against your JUP: Like Lend, you can borrow USDC from another user with JUP as collateral, at a fixed rate and for a set period. 

There's no price based liquidations, but if your loan remains unpaid after maturity, the lender can claim your JUP.

Lend USDC against JUP: Take the lender's side of the equation. If the borrower repays , you receive your principal and any interest. If they don't, you can claim their JUP collateral.

Open a leveraged long: Deposit USDC to gain more exposure to JUP's price action. 

Although this isn't technically 'earning on your JUP', it does allow you to earn on JUP's potential price appreciation.

To read more about leverage longing with Offerbook, you can check out the docs.
 

 4. Options in the Trade vertical
For completeness, its worth mentioning a couple other items:

If you're adding JUP to your portfolio, swaps from SOL or USDC via Jupiter Ultra carry a 0% platform fee. 

Additionally, you can long or short JUP on Jupiter Perps with up to 20x leverage, using USDC as collateral.

article.text:
Now live as collateral in the Backpack Market on Kamino, Backpack Securities tokenized equities give eligible holders access to USDC credit against tokens backed 1:1 by U.S.-listed shares, according to Backpack Securities.
Backpack Securities allows users to buy, sell, mint, and redeem tokenized securities backed 1:1 by real U.S.-listed stocks and ETFs on Solana. Kamino is the largest onchain lending protocol for tokenized equities by collateral deposited, with around $50 million in tokenized equities supplied as of October 2026. Through Kamino, eligible holders can borrow against those tokens while keeping price exposure to the underlying stock, subject to liquidation if the value of their collateral falls.
“Investors around the world want access to U.S. equities on their own terms, and ownership should carry the same utility onchain that it does in a brokerage account,” said Armani Ferrante, CEO of Backpack. “Backpack Securities is designed to preserve real ownership while making shares portable across Solana. Kamino’s infrastructure for  tokenized equities made it the natural venue, and integrating there gives our holders access to credit against the tokenized shares they already hold.”
1:1-backed, Redeemable Through Backpack
According to Backpack Securities, each token is issued 1:1 against an underlying share held, and eligible Backpack account holders can redeem 1:1 for that share, subject to Backpack Securities’ terms of use. Backpack Securities states that the underlying holdings are security entitlements under New York UCC Article 8, cleared and custodied by RQD Clearing, LLC and Atomic Vault Securities, LLC. Both are SEC-registered and members of FINRA and SIPC. Backpack also states that customer securities are kept separate from the company’s creditor claims.
Redemption runs through a deposit to an eligible Backpack account. Dividends are reinvested into additional tokenized shares and credited to the holder’s wallet. Splits and other corporate actions are applied through a multiplier on the token mint.
Credit Infrastructure Built for Tokenized Equities
The Backpack Market is an isolated market with its own parameters and reserves, so bad debt or liquidity shortfalls in other Kamino markets do not pass through to it. Each tokenized equity on Kamino has its own loan-to-value, liquidation, and borrow-cap parameters, set by the manager of the market where it is listed based on the liquidity and oracle coverage. The market runs onchain around the clock, and users can deposit, borrow, repay and withdraw at any time.
Backpack Securities and Kamino Expanding Credit for Tokenized Equities
The Backpack Market expands loans backed by tokenized equities on Solana. Kamino continues to build credit infrastructure for a growing range of tokenized equities, so eligible users can access liquidity against their holdings without selling them, subject to liquidation risk. As Backpack Securities expands its supported assets, additional tokenized equities are expected to come to Kamino.
“Tokenized equities become useful when they can enter credit markets with transparent onchain risk parameters,” said Michael Weisz, CEO of Kamino. “Backpack Securities has built its model around 1:1 backing and redemption, and Kamino provides the infrastructure for those assets to serve as collateral. As more of the U.S. equity market moves onchain, we expect borrowing against tokenized shares to become one of the primary ways holders use them.”
Learn more about the Backpack Market here
About Backpack Securities
Backpack Securities is a securities business building infrastructure for the convergence of traditional and digital asset markets. Through a regulated brokerage platform and a complementary tokenization platform, Backpack Securities provides investors with access to real equity ownership and blockchain-native distribution of publicly traded securities within a single portfolio experience. Since launching in June 2026, tokenized stocks issued by Backpack Securities have recorded over $6 billion in cumulative onchain trading volume and attracted more than 560,000 holders.
To learn more about Backpack, visit backpack.exchange, X, or LinkedIn.

Where a Kamino market has a third-party market manager, that manager sets the market’s parameters; Kamino does not manage, endorse, or guarantee any market manager’s parameters or risk decisions, including Allez Labs’s. article.title: Establishing the Standard for Underwriting Cross-Chain Collateral With Chainlink CCIP
article.preview: Kamino’s defense-in-depth framework combines real-time monitoring and market-level risk controls to protect the protocol. Our security review identified a proven track record and consistent security
article.text:
Kamino’s defense-in-depth framework combines real-time monitoring and market-level risk controls to protect the protocol. Our security review identified a proven track record and consistent security guarantees across chains as key reasons to support higher caps and LTVs for assets secured by Chainlink CCIP.
As Kamino onboards an increasing number of institutional tokenized assets, the infrastructure that powers them must meet the strict security standards required by capital markets. For Kamino, Chainlink’s Cross-Chain Interoperability Protocol (CCIP) is the clear choice for supporting institutional tokenized assets as collateral across chains. Its security model meets the operational standards these assets demand, giving issuers and Kamino greater confidence as we scale.
The launch of Chainlink CCIP 2.0 reinforced this decision as it provides asset issuers even more control over cross-chain transfers while retaining the common verification baseline Kamino can underwrite. Issuers are able to add their own or third-party Cross-Chain Verifiers (CCVs), apply transfer policies, and configure confirmation thresholds; any added verifier must approve a transaction alongside CCIP’s default 16 independent, security-reviewed node operators. This lets issuers tailor controls to their assets while giving Kamino a consistent starting point for due diligence.
The focus on cross-chain security extends beyond lending markets, with asset issuers and major protocols across the industry choosing Chainlink CCIP’s secure-by-default infrastructure. In August, the Wyoming Stable Token Commission, issuer of the State of Wyoming's official stable token FRNT, announced its migration from LayerZero to Chainlink CCIP. Keith Lawhorn, the Commission's Chief Information Security Officer, then went further, publicly detailing the reasons behind the move.
CCIP is designed to address these risks at the infrastructure level. Independent operators observe and validate source-chain activity, while continuous monitoring helps detect abnormal behavior and configurable rate limits constrain the value that can move if something goes wrong. Together, these safeguards give Kamino a clearer security foundation to assess as assets expand across chains.
For a lending market, this is the core issue. A lender should not have to monitor the bridge behind every cross-chain asset it accepts, build its business around that function, or carry the liability when that infrastructure fails. Given the AUM cross-chain collateral now commands, that responsibility belongs with a cross-chain solution designed, and proven, to carry it.
Why Cross-Chain Tokens Are Harder to Underwrite
A single-chain token has one primary deployment to assess and monitor. Cross-chain assets add additional dependencies across each chain and cross-chain configuration.
First, exposure surface. The token's solvency depends on the weakest mint-and-burn relationship across every chain it touches. Unbacked supply created anywhere flows freely into every market that accepts it. The exploit need not happen where the lending market sits.
Second, the review never ends. A token can be Solana-native, pass full diligence, and earn its caps, then expand to Ethereum on a bridge configuration the lending market had no part in choosing. If that configuration fails review, the options are poor: cut caps after the fact, or unwind positions on an asset that was sound when onboarded. The risk profile changed without actual changes to its underlying economic substance.
Kamino’s approach is to evaluate the cross-chain configuration itself, measuring the risk each one carries and setting caps and LTVs against what that measurement supports.
How Kamino Evaluates Cross-Chain Collateral
Cross-chain collateral is evaluated through Kamino’s existing asset risk framework. Cross-chain dependencies can affect smart contract risk, depeg risk, counterparty risk, oracle pricing risk, and market risk, with those assessments informing LTVs, caps, isolation, and asset eligibility.
Data: oracle integrity and manipulation resistance, the foundation under every liquidation.
Cross-Chain: unbacked supply, undercollateralized wrappers, and any break between a token's price and its backing, including the off-chain verification and RPC layer underneath every bridge.
Application: LTVs, liquidation thresholds and bonuses, and caps configured so an upstream failure is not profitable to exploit.
Operational Security: the compromised keys and weak controls behind most large onchain losses, which override every technical guarantee above them and are by far the most difficult to quantify.
Containment: Solvency Signals as Circuit Breakers
A lending market cannot prevent an exploit on another chain. It can refuse to be where the consequences land. The direction Kamino is building toward is to monitor solvency in real time, consuming independent signals the way it consumes price oracles, each wired to a circuit breaker. This is live today across a subset of our cross-chain assets and is being extended deliberately. It reflects where cross-chain risk management is heading, and where we intend to stay ahead of it.
The signals are concrete. A gap between a token's DEX price and its redemption or peg price means the market has learned something the backing has not. A mismatch between supply and verifiable backing means unbacked tokens are circulating. An unexplained jump in supply is the onchain shadow of a minting event elsewhere. Any of these crossing a threshold is enough to pause the market on Solana, wherever the underlying event occurred, and without waiting to establish whose infrastructure failed.
Why Standardized Validation Makes This Possible
This containment depends on signals that are trustworthy and comparable across every token, and that is what separates the two models available to issuers.
A modular model, where each issuer configures its own verifier set per lane and can change it at any time, is close to impossible to underwrite at scale. Without an enforced minimum security floor, the conservative assumption is that most issuers default to settings that remain highly centralized, because growth and risk management pull in opposite directions. Continuous oversight is not feasible when security depends on a bespoke setup the issuer controls and can alter without notice, and each token becomes its own audit, repeated every time settings change or a chain is added.
A standardized model inverts this. When every lane is secured by the same set of vetted operators, the evaluation of one token carries over to the next. Diligence is done once at the standard level, which is what turns unknown risk into measurable risk, and measurable risk into confident caps and LTVs.
Among the providers building with this model, Chainlink's CCIP carries the track record Kamino weighs most heavily today. Kamino already uses Chainlink Data Streams as a primary source of RWA pricing within Scope, alongside other providers. Separately, CCIP provides a standardized cross-chain security baseline, with a default Committee Verifier consisting of 16 independent, security-reviewed node operators, CCIP combines a standardized verification layer with configurable rate limits and emergency controls designed to limit cross-chain exposure. What stands out is what Chainlink has sustained at scale: broad issuer adoption, consistent guarantees across chains, and is the only widely used bridge that has no funds-loss exploit on its record. Our preference is for the model first, and for the providers who prove they can deliver it in production. Chainlink has done that work, and our alignment reflects it.
What This Means in Practice
Greater uncertainty in a token's cross-chain posture demands a higher onboarding bar, and where risk cannot be validated, exposure comes down. Tokens on standardized, secure-by-default infrastructure, such as Chainlink CCIP, earn higher caps and LTVs because their risk can be quantified. Tokens on bespoke, per-lane configurations face heavier diligence, lower caps, and in some cases rejection or delisting, as a reflection of what can be measured rather than a judgment on the issuer.
To issuers planning cross-chain expansion: choose infrastructure that lets a lending market underwrite you once and trust the result across every chain you touch.

article.text:
Kamino Fixed Rates bring a defined cost of capital and duration to onchain leverage, where financing has historically been dominated by variable-rate, open-term borrowing. This lets borrowers structure leveraged positions around known funding costs rather than utilization-driven rate changes.
With Fixed Rate Multiply, a user selects an asset and target leverage, and Kamino builds the position in one transaction. The debt comes from a fixed-rate reserve, locking the financing cost for the full term, while Auto Rollover can carry the position into another eligible fixed term at expiry without requiring manual refinancing.
The first Fixed Rate Multiply vault, AUTO/wYLDS, went live on September 21 with Figure and HastraFi. Since launch, the broader AUTO Market has scaled to $35M in fixed-rate loans, while AUTO supply has grown from $9M to $55M.
How Fixed Rate Multiply Works
Fixed Rate Multiply uses Kamino’s existing one-click leverage flow, but the borrow is originated at a fixed rate for a defined term instead of at a variable rate.
A user selects an asset and target leverage, and Kamino builds the position in a single transaction:
A flash loan provides the capital needed to reach the target leverage
The initial deposit and flash-borrowed funds are converted into the collateral asset
The full amount is deposited into Kamino as collateral
The debt asset is borrowed from a fixed-rate reserve and used to repay the flash loan
The result is a leveraged position with a financing cost that is fixed for the full term.
If any step fails, the transaction reverts and no position is created. Closing runs the same flow in reverse. The flash loan fee is 0.001% per transaction.
 
What Does a Fixed Rate Change?
Fixed Rate Multiply gives leveraged strategies a defined cost of capital over a defined period.
Instead of borrowing from a variable-rate reserve, the position borrows from a reserve configured for a specific asset, rate, and term. Once the loan is originated, that rate remains fixed through the end of the term, regardless of changes in utilization elsewhere.
Today, AUTO/wYLDS uses three 30-day wYLDS reserves at 5.30%, 5.75%, and 6%. Each reserve has its own available liquidity, and borrowers access that liquidity directly when opening a Fixed Rate position.
As Kamino expands Fixed Rates across additional terms and markets, these reserves can form the basis of a broader onchain yield curve.
Fixed-term borrowing also introduces different tradeoffs from open-term variable credit. Fixed rates can price at a premium to the prevailing variable rate, and closing during the initial term may incur an Early Repay Penalty to compensate lenders that committed capital for that duration. After the first rollover, positions can be closed without that additional penalty.
AUTO/wYLDS
AUTO is a yield-bearing token, backed by near-prime U.S. auto loans originated by Agora Data, structured through Figure Forge, and minted through HastraFi. The AUTO/wYLDS vault deposits AUTO as collateral, borrows wYLDS at a fixed rate, and loops the borrowed capital back into AUTO, maintaining USD-denominated exposure. Entry and exit route through Figure’s mint and redeem infrastructure rather than relying on secondary-market liquidity.
 
Auto Rollover: Carrying Positions Across Fixed Terms
Fixed-rate credit becomes significantly more useful onchain when borrowers can manage duration without rebuilding positions at every expiry.
Three days before the end date, a position enters its rollover window. If eligible fixed-rate liquidity is available, the loan can move into a new term automatically instead of requiring the borrower to close and manually refinance.
At expiry, Kamino follows the available path in order:
Roll into another eligible fixed term: If qualifying fixed-rate liquidity is available, the position continues into a new term.
Move into the variable-rate reserve where supported: If a fixed-rate rollover is unavailable, the debt can fall back to variable borrowing for the same asset in the same market.
Auto-repay: If neither path is available, the protocol begins repaying the debt from collateral according to the market’s configured Auto-repay mechanics.
 
Auto Rollover gives borrowers the defined cost of capital of fixed-term credit without turning every maturity into a manual refinancing event.
Users can disable rollover from the position interface, and the position lifecycle shows the active term, rollover window and expected expiry path.
Liquidations
A fixed rate removes financing-rate volatility during the active term. It does not remove collateral or liquidation risk.
AUTO/wYLDS has a maximum LTV of 78% and a liquidation LTV of 80%. A position opened near maximum leverage therefore has less room for relative movement between AUTO and wYLDS before reaching the liquidation threshold.
AUTO continues to accrue yield while interest accrues on the wYLDS debt. As long as AUTO’s yield remains above the fixed borrow rate and the relative value of the two assets remains stable, LTV should decline over the term. If that spread reverses or AUTO falls relative to wYLDS, LTV can increase.
Fixed Rate Multiply makes the financing cost predictable, but collateral performance, position sizing and liquidation risk still need to be managed throughout the term.
Defined Cost of Capital with Continuity Across Terms
Fixed Rates introduce a new function to onchain leverage: the ability to finance a position at a known cost for a defined period while maintaining continuity across maturities.
A borrower can calculate the financing spread at entry, size the position against that cost and hold through the term without the borrow rate repricing with utilization. As the term approaches expiry, Auto Rollover can carry the position into another eligible fixed term rather than forcing the borrower to rebuild it manually.
Fixed Rate Multiply packages that infrastructure into the same one-click experience already used for leveraged strategies across Kamino.
AUTO/wYLDS is the first Fixed Rate Multiply vault. From here, Kamino is expanding Fixed Rates across new markets and reserves, while adding new functionality around term selection, rollover and fixed-rate liquidity. As that infrastructure develops, a broader range of strategies will be able to access defined financing directly onchain.
Learn more: kamino.com/docs/products/borrow/fixed-rates
